quote: E. T. Jaynes used the term Mind Projection Fallacy to denote the error of projecting your own mind’s properties into the external world.
content: Jaynes coined the phrase (in Probability Theory: The Logic of Science and a 1989 lecture), but the idea is Hume’s, and before Hume, Locke’s. The primary/secondary quality distinction (Locke, Essay, II.viii) is exactly the claim that colours, tastes and the like are powers to produce ideas in observers rather than resemblances in the object, and Hume’s description of the mind’s “propensity to spread itself on external objects” (Treatise, I.iii.14) and taste’s habit of “gilding or staining all natural objects with the colours borrowed from internal sentiment” (Enquiry Concerning the Principles of Morals, Appendix I) is the essay’s torn-dress example with beauty in place of sexiness. The essay attributes the fallacy to Kant and Hume as perpetrators in the next paragraph while presenting their thesis as Jaynes’s. There is also a substantive dispute the essay does not enter. On the response-dependence account of secondary qualities (Wright, “Moral Values, Projection and Secondary Qualities,” Proceedings of the Aristotelian Society, Supplementary Volume, 1988; Johnston (1989)), “sexy” means something like “disposed to elicit attraction in normal observers,” and attributing it to the woman is as correct as attributing redness to a tomato; the artist’s only mistake is about which observers are normal. On that account, projection is not a fallacy but the correct semantics for a whole class of predicates, and the essay assumes the answer to a live question in order to name the fallacy.

quote: and Kant’s declaration that space by its very nature is flat, and Hume’s definition of a priori ideas as those “discoverable by the mere operation of thought, without dependence on what is anywhere existent in the universe”…
content: Both examples are misdescribed, and Kant is the reverse of the essay’s fallacy. Kant did not declare that space “by its very nature” is flat; he held that Euclidean geometry is synthetic a priori because space is a form of human intuition, that is, a feature of the mind that structures experience, not a property of things in themselves (Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Aesthetic). That is the thesis that geometry is in the map. One can fault Kant for thinking the map’s geometry was fixed, but the one thing he did not do was project it onto the territory; the noumenal world, for Kant, has no spatial properties at all. In his 1746 Thoughts on the True Estimation of Living Forces (§§9–11) he had already speculated that other dimensionalities of space were possible and that ours follows from the inverse-square law. Hume’s sentence, from the Enquiry §IV, is a definition of “relations of ideas” as against “matters of fact,” and it is the founding statement of the distinction that makes the essay’s own separation of “probability theory” (a priori, theorems) from empirical claims possible. Naming Hume as an instance of the fallacy while borrowing the fallacy from him is the sort of thing that happens when history is recalled in the shape of the argument.

quote: Apparently we instinctively represent Sexiness as a direct attribute of the Woman data structure, Woman.sexiness, like Woman.height or Woman.weight.
content: This is offered as an observation and it is a hypothesis about cognitive architecture with no evidence attached, and the evidence that exists points the other way. Children distinguish response-dependent from response-independent properties early: by around age five they judge that a food can be tasty to one person and not to another while a rock’s weight cannot (Flavell, Flavell, Green & Moses, “Young children’s understanding of fact beliefs versus value beliefs,” Child Development 61, 1990), which is the distinction the data structure is supposed to lack. Adults know perfectly well that attractiveness varies by observer; what the pulp cover shows is that an illustrator painting for an audience of human males painted what that audience found attractive, and the alien is a prop. The essay reads the cover as a specimen of the artist’s theory of alien psychology, and the only evidence for the theory is the cover. This is the pattern Book III’s annotations found throughout the evolutionary-psychology essays, a mechanism drawn to fit one example, and it is applied here to an example whose simpler explanation is commercial.
